lessonTitle: Common Inflammatory Skin Disease: Eczema, Psoriasis and Acne

blocks.text: A 9-year-old boy scratches through the night. His mother points to red, rough, crusted patches in the creases of his elbows and behind his knees, and says that his skin has always been dry. At the next clinic a 45-year-old man has sharply edged red plaques with silvery scale on his elbows and knees. Both are 'rashes', but a precise description is what separates the two diagnoses and shapes treatment.

blocks.markdown: Dermatology is a visual discipline with a precise vocabulary. A **primary lesion** is the basic change the disease produces; a **secondary lesion** results from evolution, scratching, rubbing or treatment. Describe any rash by **morphology** (what it looks like), **distribution** (where it is and whether it is symmetrical), **configuration** (linear, annular, grouped) and **associated features** (itch, pain, nails, joints, mucosa). Naming the lesion correctly narrows the differential before any test is done.

blocks.title: Standard morphological terms
blocks.text: **Macule**: flat colour change under 1 cm; **patch**: flat colour change 1 cm or more. **Papule**: raised solid lesion under 1 cm; **plaque**: raised, flat-topped lesion 1 cm or more; **nodule**: deeper, palpable solid lesion. **Vesicle**: fluid-filled blister under 1 cm; **bulla**: 1 cm or more; **pustule**: pus-filled lesion. Secondary changes: **scale**, **crust**, **excoriation**, **erosion**, **ulcer**, **fissure**, **lichenification** (thickened skin with exaggerated markings from chronic rubbing) and **scar**. Size cut-offs of 1 cm are the usual convention.

blocks.title: Describing a lesion
blocks.prompt: On the elbow of a 45-year-old man you find a well-demarcated, red, raised area 3 cm across, with thick silvery-white flakes on the surface. How do you describe it?

steps.text: Is it flat or raised? Raised and palpable: papule, plaque or nodule.
Size is 3 cm, which is over 1 cm, and the surface is flat-topped: a plaque rather than a papule.
The surface layer is flakes of stratum corneum: scale. The edge is sharp: well-demarcated. The colour is erythematous.
Complete description: a 3 cm well-demarcated erythematous plaque with silvery scale on the extensor aspect of the elbow, which is the typical description of chronic plaque psoriasis.

blocks.answer: A 3 cm well-demarcated erythematous scaly plaque on the extensor elbow.

blocks.markdown: **Eczema** (dermatitis) is an inflammatory skin disease characterised by itch, erythema, dryness, scale and, in acute phases, vesicles and weeping; chronic rubbing causes lichenification and excoriations. **Atopic eczema** is the commonest form and results from a defective skin barrier (for example filaggrin mutations) with immune dysregulation, often in people with asthma or allergic rhinitis. In young children it affects the face and extensor surfaces, and from later childhood and in adults it classically involves the **flexures** (antecubital and popliteal fossae, neck, wrists, eyelids). The borders are ill-defined and itch is prominent. Other forms include contact (irritant or allergic) dermatitis, seborrhoeic dermatitis and discoid eczema.

**Psoriasis** is a chronic immune-mediated disease with accelerated epidermal turnover and T-cell driven inflammation. **Chronic plaque psoriasis** presents with sharply demarcated, erythematous plaques with silvery scale on the **extensor surfaces** (elbows, knees), scalp, sacrum and umbilicus. Scraping the scale reveals pinpoint bleeding (Auspitz sign). Trauma can trigger new lesions in normal skin (Koebner phenomenon). **Nail involvement** (pitting, onycholysis) and **psoriatic arthritis** are important associations. **Guttate psoriasis** (numerous small drop-shaped lesions) often follows streptococcal sore throat. Psoriasis is associated with cardiovascular disease and metabolic syndrome.

rows: Flexures (adults and older children); face and extensors in infants
Dry, excoriated, lichenified, may weep or crust
Atopy: asthma, hay fever; family history
Nail pitting, psoriatic arthritis, Koebner phenomenon, cardiovascular risk
blocks.caption: Eczema versus psoriasis by distribution and appearance.

blocks.markdown: **Acne vulgaris** affects the pilosebaceous unit and is driven by raised sebum production under androgen influence, follicular hyperkeratinisation (forming comedones), colonisation by *Cutibacterium acnes* and inflammation. It presents on the face, chest and back with open and closed comedones, inflammatory papules and pustules and, in severe cases, nodules and cysts that scar. First-line treatment for mild to moderate acne is topical: a topical retinoid (for example adapalene) and/or benzoyl peroxide, often as a fixed combination. Topical or oral antibiotics are not used alone because of resistance; if oral antibiotics are used (for example a tetracycline) they are combined with a topical non-antibiotic agent and reviewed at around 3 months. Severe, scarring or refractory disease is referred for **isotretinoin**, which is teratogenic and requires a pregnancy prevention programme (check current MHRA and BNF guidance).

blocks.caption: One fingertip unit (FTU) is the amount of topical steroid squeezed from a standard 5 mm nozzle from the distal skin crease to the tip of an adult index finger, about 0.5 g, and covers an area about twice the size of an adult hand (flat, fingers together). Use for quantity estimates only.

blocks.title: Estimating the steroid quantity
blocks.prompt: A patient is prescribed a once-daily topical corticosteroid for an area of eczema equal to 8 adult hand areas. How much is needed per application and how long will a 30 g tube last?

steps.text: Each FTU covers 2 hand areas, so the FTUs needed per application are:
Convert to grams at 0.5 g per FTU:
A 30 g tube at one application per day:
This helps prescribers supply an adequate quantity, avoiding under-treatment from fear of steroids and over-use. Always follow BNF and local guidance on potency, site and duration.

blocks.answer: 2.0 g per application; a 30 g tube lasts about 15 days of once-daily use.

blocks.markdown: **Topical treatment principles.** **Emollients** are the foundation for eczema and are also useful in psoriasis: apply liberally and frequently (several times a day), use as soap substitutes, and apply in the direction of hair growth. **Topical corticosteroids** are used for flares, matching **potency** to site, age and severity: mild for the face, flexures and infants; moderate or potent for the trunk and limbs; very potent only for short courses on thick palmar or plantar skin under specialist direction. Use the lowest effective potency for the shortest time, and the right quantity (fingertip units). Risks are skin atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, perioral dermatitis and, with prolonged or extensive use, systemic absorption. **Psoriasis** topical therapy includes potent steroids, vitamin D analogues (calcipotriol), tar and dithranol; calcineurin inhibitors (for example tacrolimus) are alternatives in eczema on sensitive sites under specialist advice.

rows: Specialist or short-term use on palms and soles
blocks.caption: Topical corticosteroid potency ladder. Preparations and indications must be checked against the BNF.

items: Extensive disease, for example more than 10 percent of body surface area in psoriasis, or severe eczema not controlled by optimal topical therapy.
Disease on sites that are disabling or hard to treat (face, hands, genitals, palms and soles, nails) or with marked impact on quality of life (dermatology life quality index (DLQI) scores).
Failure of topical therapy, or frequent flares needing repeated potent steroid courses.
Erythroderma, generalised pustular psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis (urgent specialist care).

Options include phototherapy (narrowband UVB), methotrexate, ciclosporin, acitretin and biologic therapies for psoriasis; in eczema, phototherapy, methotrexate, ciclosporin and selected biologic or targeted agents. Initiation is specialist-led.

blocks.title: Describe before you diagnose
blocks.text: Name the lesion, site, border and surface. Itchy, ill-defined, flexural and excoriated suggests eczema; sharply demarcated, silvery scaly extensor plaques with nail changes suggest psoriasis. Treatment follows the stepped ladder: emollient, appropriately potent topical steroid or targeted topical, then systemic therapy when topicals fail or disease is extensive.

points: Describe skin lesions using primary terms (macule, patch, papule, plaque, nodule, vesicle, bulla, pustule) and secondary terms (scale, crust, excoriation, lichenification), plus site and distribution.
Eczema is itchy, ill-defined and flexural; psoriasis is sharply demarcated with silvery scale on extensor surfaces and nail changes; acne involves comedones, papules and pustules.
Topical therapy uses emollients and potency-matched steroids in adequate quantity; systemic or phototherapy is considered for extensive, disabling or refractory disease.

questions.stem: A dermatologist notes a 12 mm raised, flat-topped, scaly red lesion on a patient's shin. Which morphological term applies?

distractorRationale.a: A macule is flat and not palpable.
distractorRationale.b: A papule is raised but under 1 cm.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: raised, flat-topped lesions of 1 cm or more are plaques.
distractorRationale.d: A vesicle is a fluid-filled blister under 1 cm.

questions.explanation: Raised lesions are classified by size: under 1 cm is a papule and 1 cm or more with a flat top is a plaque. A 12 mm lesion that is raised and scaly is therefore a plaque.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman develops, over 10 days, dozens of small 3 to 5 mm drop-shaped pink scaly papules across the trunk and proximal limbs, two weeks after a sore throat. There is little itch. Which diagnosis is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Atopic eczema is itchy and flexural with ill-defined margins, not scattered drop-shaped scaly papules.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: guttate psoriasis classically follows a streptococcal sore throat and causes numerous small scaly papules with little itch.
distractorRationale.c: Contact dermatitis follows the pattern of exposure and is itchy.
distractorRationale.d: Acne affects the pilosebaceous areas of face, chest and back with comedones.

questions.explanation: Guttate psoriasis is an acute eruption of small scaly drop-shaped lesions that often follows streptococcal pharyngitis in young people. It is a form of psoriasis rather than eczema, and is typically not very itchy.

questions.stem: A 7-month-old infant has a moderate flare of atopic eczema on the cheeks and neck folds. Which topical corticosteroid approach is most appropriate alongside regular emollients?

options.text: A very potent steroid for 4 weeks
A mild-potency steroid such as hydrocortisone 1% for a short course
A potent steroid daily on the face

questions.correctOptionText: A mild-potency steroid such as hydrocortisone 1% for a short course

distractorRationale.a: Very potent steroids on infant facial skin risk atrophy and systemic absorption.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: mild potency on the face and flexures, for the shortest time, with emollients (check BNF and local guidance).
distractorRationale.c: Potent steroids are avoided on the face in infants.
distractorRationale.d: Untreated flares cause distress and infection; appropriate mild steroids are safe.

questions.explanation: Potency is matched to site and age. The face and skin folds absorb more steroid, so a mild steroid for a short course is used with liberal emollients.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman has chronic plaque psoriasis covering about 25 percent of her body surface area. Despite 3 months of correct topical therapy her DLQI score is high and her work is affected. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue the same topical therapy indefinitely
Refer to dermatology to consider phototherapy or systemic therapy
Switch to a very potent steroid on all areas
Stop all treatment and review in a year

questions.correctOptionText: Refer to dermatology to consider phototherapy or systemic therapy

distractorRationale.a: Persistent disease despite adequate topical therapy needs escalation.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: extensive disease with failure of topical therapy and high quality-of-life impact is an indication for specialist systemic or phototherapy.
distractorRationale.c: Very potent steroids over large areas risk systemic absorption.
distractorRationale.d: No treatment would leave the disease and its burden unaddressed.

questions.explanation: Extensive or refractory psoriasis and significant impact on quality of life are indications to consider phototherapy or systemic treatment in specialist care. Large-area very potent steroids are inappropriate.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old has mild to moderate acne with open and closed comedones and several inflammatory papules and pustules on the face. Which first-line topical regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: A topical retinoid such as adapalene, benzoyl peroxide, or a fixed combination of the two
A topical antibiotic used alone for 6 months

questions.correctOptionText: A topical retinoid such as adapalene, benzoyl peroxide, or a fixed combination of the two

distractorRationale.a: Correct: topical retinoid and/or benzoyl peroxide address comedones and inflammation and limit antibiotic resistance.
distractorRationale.b: Isotretinoin is for severe or refractory disease and is specialist-initiated.

questions.explanation: Mild to moderate acne is treated with topical retinoid and/or benzoyl peroxide. Antibiotics are not used alone because of resistance, and isotretinoin is reserved for severe disease under specialist supervision.

questions.stem: Atopic eczema in adults typically affects the extensor surfaces of the elbows and knees with sharply demarcated, silvery scaly plaques.
questions.explanation: This description fits psoriasis. Adult atopic eczema classically involves the flexures, with ill-defined, itchy, dry or lichenified skin and excoriations.

questions.stem: A patient is prescribed a once-daily topical corticosteroid for eczema affecting an area equal to 6 adult hand areas. One fingertip unit (0.5 g) covers about 2 adult hand areas. How many grams are needed for 7 days of once-daily application?
questions.explanation: FTUs per application = 6/2 = 3 FTU. Grams per application = 3 x 0.5 = 1.5 g. Over 7 days the total is 1.5 x 7 = 10.5 g. Estimating quantity helps ensure adequate treatment (check the BNF and local guidance for duration and potency).

questions.stem: Using standard terminology, describe the lesions of (a) a patient with excoriated, thickened skin in the antecubital fossae and (b) a patient with a sharply demarcated erythematous scaly lesion 4 cm in diameter on the knee. Define the terms you use.
markingGuide: Define primary lesions by size: macule/patch, papule/plaque, nodule, vesicle/bulla, pustule; and secondary lesions such as scale, crust, excoriation, lichenification
(a) Lichenified plaques with excoriations (scratch marks) in the flexures
Lichenification: thickened skin with accentuated markings from chronic rubbing
(b) A well-demarcated erythematous scaly plaque (greater than 1 cm, raised, flat-topped)
Mention site/distribution and border as part of the description
Link to likely diagnoses: atopic eczema and plaque psoriasis
questions.explanation: Accurate morphological language narrows the differential. Size and elevation distinguish plaques from papules, and secondary changes reveal chronicity and scratching.

questions.stem: Contrast atopic eczema with chronic plaque psoriasis in terms of distribution, appearance, symptoms and associations.
markingGuide: Eczema: itch prominent, ill-defined borders, flexural distribution (adults, older children), dry or lichenified skin with excoriation
Psoriasis: sharply demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale, extensor surfaces, scalp, sacrum
Eczema associations: atopy, asthma, hay fever, family history, skin barrier defect
Psoriasis associations: nail pitting, psoriatic arthritis, Koebner phenomenon, cardiovascular risk
Mention Auspitz sign and guttate psoriasis following streptococcal infection
Infantile eczema affects face and extensor surfaces
questions.explanation: Distribution, border and surface scale are the quickest discriminators. Associations help with the diagnosis and with screening for comorbidity.

questions.stem: Outline the principles of topical treatment of eczema and psoriasis and describe when systemic therapy or phototherapy is considered.
markingGuide: Emollients as foundation for eczema (liberal and frequent, soap substitute)
Topical corticosteroids matched to potency, site, age and severity; mild on face/flexures; use lowest effective potency for shortest time; fingertip units for quantity
Adverse effects: atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, perioral dermatitis, systemic absorption
Psoriasis topical options: potent steroid, vitamin D analogue, tar, dithranol
Systemic or phototherapy considered for extensive disease, disabling sites, failure of topical therapy, severe quality-of-life impact, erythroderma, pustular disease, psoriatic arthritis
Examples: narrowband UVB, methotrexate, ciclosporin, acitretin, biologics; specialist-initiated
questions.explanation: Treatment is stepped. The key judgement is matching potency and quantity to site and age, and recognising when topical therapy has failed or disease burden justifies specialist systemic treatment.
